newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU timetable to overshadow ministerial talks. [CORRECTED 15:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EMU timetable to overshadow ministerial talks. [CORRECTED 15:25 GMT]

text.p: European Union finance ministers, deluged in recent weeks by speculation about a delay in the starting date for a single currency, will get a chance this weekend to reinstill confidence in their plans for monetary union.

Meeting in the Dutch seaside town of Noordwijk, the informal session of ministers and central bankers on Saturday will review progress on some of the more technical aspects of economic and monetary union (EMU).

But such mundane details, while important, are likely to take a back seat to the more pressing concerns of sluggish European growth, rising joblessness and the battle that many governments are having in meeting the preconditions for EMU.
In this regard, attention will be focused squarely on Germany.

Record unemployment and doubts over the speed at which the German economy will expand in the near future have fuelled concern that Bonn might be unable to abide strictly by the Maastricht treaty's criteria on deficits and debt.
Countries wishing to join EMU, scheduled to start in 1999, must bring their 1997 budget deficits close to three percent of gross domestic product.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has repeatedly said strict interpretation of the criteria must come before the timetable, a position that has offered markets an opportunity to believe that a delayed starting date is not that far-fetched.
Although most analysts expect EU finance ministers to reaffirm their commitment to the 1999 deadline, widespread worries over Germany's fiscal health are not likely to be assuaged this weekend.

"I think we just have to wait and see if Germany shows the kind of economic rebound we are expecting and, if the budget falls short, whether Bonn comes through with any additional measures," said Bruce Kasman, economist at J.P. Morgan in London.
One important element of the weekend gathering, say analysts, is whether ministers and central bankers show any cracks in their resolve on meeting the 1999 launch date.
Such a development, seen by many as unlikely, would give investors a potent reason for betting heavily on a delay.

The ministers will try to set a date for the decision on which countries join EMU. The heavy betting is on late April 1998, well after the French parliamentary election (corrects from "presidential election") and the earliest possible opportunity, given the logistics of EU decision-making.

Before the decision is taken, several hurdles must be overcome, including reports by the European Commission and the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute (EMI) on the degree of economic convergence within the 15-nation bloc.
Reliable economic data for 1997, used to make the assessment, is expected towards the end of February 1998.
Once available, both the Commission and the EMI -- forerunner to a European Central Bank -- will need about two weeks to assess how each country stands in relation to the Maastricht criteria.

After the evaluation, a further six weeks are needed for consultation with the European Parliament, whose views are not in any way binding. It is after this period that a decision on EMU members will be taken.
The ministers will also receive an update on negotiations to put a stability and growth pact into a legal context.
The pact, which seeks to penalise governments running excessive budget deficits -- above three percent of GDP -- inside EMU, was agreed last December after lengthy and often tense negotiations.
No difficulties are anticipated on this front, although diplomats said a few outstanding points needed to be resolved.
The group will also take stock of negotiations on a revamped Exchange Rate Mechanism, dubbed ERM 2, and designed to link countries outside EMU to the single currency, the euro.
Here again, many expressed confidence that any outstanding points could be resolved quickly and without rancour.
The results of Saturday's meeting are expected to set the stage for final adoption by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam in June.
